newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU WILLING TO COMPROMISE IN NORDIC ALCOHOL TALKS.
newsitem.headline: EU WILLING TO COMPROMISE IN NORDIC ALCOHOL TALKS.

text.p: The Commission told Sweden on Monday it was willing to compromise in talks on phasing out rules which allow the country to limit the amount of alcohol Swedes may bring back home from elsewhere in the bloc, but stressed that in the end the import restrictions must end.
Internal Market Commissioner Mario Monti held talks on Monday on the sensitive issue with Swedish Taxation Minister Thomas Ostros, but without reaching any conclusions.
"We are pushing for a compromise, we are ready to be flexible," a Commission official told reporters after the talks. "I think a solution must be found quite soon."

The Commission wants the restrictions to end because it says they go against the internal market -- where goods are supposed to flow freely -- while Sweden wants to keep them because of health- and tax-reasons.
The negotiations will continue this autumn. Denmark and Finland also seek to keep similar rules on alcohol imports.

However, if there is no deal this year the case may have to be settled by the European Court of Justice and then the restrictions may have to end immediately rather than being phased out, the official said.
"We really want to avoid confrontation," the Commission official said, adding, however, that it would be difficult to avoid a court ruling if there was no deal by January.
A phase out could be one way to solve the issue, gradually allowing people to bring in more alcohol while at the same giving the three Nordics time to prepare for the new rules, the official said.

Denmark, Sweden and Finland all have exemptions from EU rules so that they can restrict personal alcohol imports, but these will expire by the end of 1996 unless there is a new agreement -- at least according to the Commission.
The official said the Commission was ready to give the three Nordics "as much as possible" in the talks but added: "We need to have have a final date on ending this derogation."
The issue is politically highly sensitive for the Nordic states which have a traditional policy of high taxes on alcohol as part of efforts to reduce excessive drinking.
It is also a question of fiscal importance. In Sweden, taxes on alcohol and tobacco bring in a total of 18 billion crowns annually in state revenue.
The Nordic states would prefer to hold on to their derogations from EU rules as long as possible.
As Nordic excise duties on alcohol are much higher than elsewhere in the EU, some fear individual alcohol imports would jump if they lost their right to restrict imports.
Sweden and Finland won the right to limit alcohol imports during the accession negotiations in 1994, linking this to a Danish deal struck two years earlier.
Under current rules, a Swede is allowed to take home up to one litre of spirits, five litres of wine and 15 litres of beer.
